rows.evidence: Both versions retain all seven concerns, four suggestions, locations, conditions, and requested verification, including explicit refs, alias handling, legacy typed values, UUID-named output, and per-lookup cache results. A's neutral summary and compact issue/action tables read more naturally than B's mechanized COMMENT framing and repeated finding IDs, despite B surfacing the action list more immediately.

Both preserve the canonical-model-alias defect and the pinned-snapshot/source-derived-fallback boundary. B connects cause and effect in one natural sentence and gives the same complete action without extra presentation scaffolding.

Both retain explicit branch and tag refs, the commit-SHA requirement, and the no-network offline-replay boundary. B's direct “Pin” instruction and compact causal wording are easier to absorb and remember.

Both fully identify the stale argument namespace, pre-conversion failure, parser change, and offline defaults test. A makes the two actions easier to scan; B is more conversational and compact, with no substantive readability advantage overall.

Both preserve the populated-value condition, finite metric-rule validation, publication consequence, and routing of invalid rows to SourceConversionResult. A separates the two fixes for recall; B expresses them more naturally in one sentence.

Both retain the new-snapshot pinned-content action and the strict legacy behavior: leave the typed value unset and mark missing content. A states the complete defect and two-era remedy plainly without unnecessary headings.

Both identify locally present missing/null entries as the skipped live-lookup case and preserve unchanged offline behavior. B explains the skip and resulting inability to discover a newly available value in one smoother sentence.
Both preserve exact-canonical-ID precedence and the unique-owner restriction on normalized resolution. B is shorter and more direct while retaining the collision consequence.

Both retain every concern, boundary, and test purpose: preflight and recoverable old files through successful writes and route transitions, multi-route mid-write rollback tests, raw-source identity, finite-number worker accounting, atomic report publication, and limit semantics. B's neutral overview and full-detail tables are calmer and less repetitive than A's generated-result framing and ID-heavy bullets.

Both preserve the deletion timing, rollback boundary, recoverable-old-file requirement through every successful write and route transition, and the multi-route mid-write test's rollback purpose. B's three-item action list is materially easier to scan and recall.

Both preserve the alias-redirect identity instability and the metadata/routing boundary. B more explicitly labels the raw dataset path as the original source value and says the reconciled repository remains unchanged, making the requested split harder to misread.

Both retain exclusions-only accounting, stale-report risk, post-publication atomic replacement, clean-run coverage, and preservation of the last complete report. B's heading exposes the triggering run state immediately and its action clearly names fully clean runs.

Both preserve the PR #221/rebase condition, default-rich CLI verification, exact guide path and its three required topics, plus all four qualified suggestions. A's neutral summary and issue/action tables are simpler and more human than B's COMMENT/merge-readiness framing and generated finding IDs; no credit is given for B's merge judgment.

Both preserve why PASS hides the warning, PR #221 as the prerequisite, rebase timing, and the default-rich CLI check of the complete path. A presents the causal chain and follow-up as two natural paragraphs without fragmenting them into four blocks.

Both retain the exact required guide, the missing update, and all three documentation requirements: alias trigger, warning-only result, and single-record evidence limit. A is complete in two concise, natural paragraphs; B repeats the repository-rule setup with little added clarity.
